extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning introductory sentential and quantificational logic (discrete math / symbolic logic courses)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, equivalences, and translation conventions for sentential (conditional, biconditional) connectives and first-order quantifiers; guidance for translating English into logical formulas and for using truth tables to evaluate validity and truth of quantified statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional truth table / conditional law
rubrics_metrics.description: The conditional P -> Q is equivalent to ¬P ∨ Q; it is false exactly when P is true and Q is false (true in all other cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the truth table for P -> Q in validity analyses of arguments. Changing entries (e.g., making P -> Q false in the first or second line) would lead to unreasonable validity judgments. Examples: teacher threat example (¬P ∨ Q vs intended meaning P -> Q), and algebra example (P(x) -> Q(x) equivalent to ¬(P(x) ∧ ¬Q(x))).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional equivalence: ¬(P ∧ ¬Q)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form emphasizes that P -> Q is true whenever there is no case with P true and Q false; used to explain why universally true conditionals can be rephrased as negated conjunctions. Example: 'If x>2 then x^2>4' true because there is no x with x>2 and x^2≤4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrapositive law
rubrics_metrics.description: P -> Q is equivalent to ¬Q -> ¬P (the contrapositive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equivalence is often used in mathematical reasoning and proofs (example: 'If John cashed the check then my account is overdrawn' equivalent to 'If my account isn't overdrawn then John hasn't cashed the check').

rubrics_metrics.name: Converse is not equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: The converse Q -> P is not equivalent to P -> Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: do not confuse a conditional with its converse. Example: 'If convicted murderer then untrustworthy' does not imply 'If untrustworthy then convicted murderer.' Check with truth tables if unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biconditional definition and meaning (iff)
rubrics_metrics.description: P ↔ Q (P iff Q) is defined as (P -> Q) ∧ (Q -> P); it expresses necessary and sufficient conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common abbreviation: iff. Equivalent forms include (P ∧ Q) ∨ (¬P ∧ ¬Q) (derivable using equivalences). In mathematics, use explicit 'iff' or 'necessary and sufficient' when a biconditional is intended; do not assume everyday 'if' implies biconditional.

rubrics_metrics.name: English phrasings that correspond to P -> Q
rubrics_metrics.description: Common English forms that mean P -> Q include: 'P implies Q', 'Q, if P', 'P only if Q', 'P is a sufficient condition for Q', 'Q is a necessary condition for P'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate carefully: e.g., 'P only if Q' is equivalent to P -> Q (since it says if not Q then not P). Use contrapositive to check translations. Examples provided: 'You can run for president only if you are a citizen' → P -> Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation guidance: rephrase and translate in steps
rubrics_metrics.description: When translating English sentences into formulas, rewrite awkward phrasings into 'if ... then ...' forms and translate piecewise, introducing predicate symbols and names as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended stepwise method: identify quantifier words (everyone, someone), rephrase complex relational statements (e.g., 'x is married' as ∃y M(x,y)), introduce letters for specific individuals (s for Susan), and avoid reusing bound-variable names to reduce confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth-table method for argument validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use truth tables to test validity: an argument is valid iff in every row where all premises are true the conclusion is also true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: showing why {P, P -> Q} ⊢ Q is valid (both premises true only in a row where conclusion true), and why {P -> Q, Q} ⊬ P is invalid (counterexample row exists). The conditional truth table entries are essential to these evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifier: universal (∀) meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: ∀x P(x) means 'for all x, P(x)' — P(x) is true for every element of the universe of discourse; equivalently, the truth set of P(x) equals the whole universe U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation examples: ∀x (x^2 > 0) over R, and explanation of when such universal claims are true or false by checking possible counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifier: existential (∃) meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: ∃x P(x) means 'there exists an x such that P(x)' — there is at least one element in the universe for which P(x) is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation examples: ∃x (x^2 − 2x + 3 = 0) over R is false because the equation has no real solutions; use truth-set intuition (nonempty vs empty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifier scope convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantifier expressions ∀x and ∃x apply only to the statement that comes immediately after them unless parentheses indicate otherwise (e.g., ∀x P(x) -> Q(x) is parsed as (∀x P(x)) -> Q(x), not ∀x (P(x) -> Q(x))).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with parentheses and implicit scope; when in doubt, add parentheses to make intended scope explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bound vs free variables and renaming
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantifiers bind variables; a bound variable can be replaced by a fresh variable without changing meaning. Variables not bound by a quantifier in a formula are free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use renaming to avoid confusion when nesting quantifiers or combining quantified formulas (example: replace repeated bound variable y with z to avoid collision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressing relational predicates with quantifiers (nested quantifiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: To express relational statements use additional quantifiers: e.g., 'x is married' can be represented as ∃y M(x,y), and 'some students are married' as ∃x (S(x) ∧ ∃y M(x,y)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating statements like 'All parents are married', consider representing 'parent' and 'married' as relations and avoid variable confusion by renaming bound variables: ∀x (∃y P(x,y) -> ∃z M(x,z)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of quantifiers matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The order of quantifiers can change meaning: ∀x ∃y P(x,y) generally differs from ∃y ∀x P(x,y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ∀x ∃y (x + y = 5) is true in R (for each x choose y = 5 − x), but ∃y ∀x (x + y = 5) is false. When analyzing multiquantifier statements, process quantifiers one at a time and test by plugging values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting universal quantifier applied to a conditional
rubrics_metrics.description: A formula of the form ∀x (S(x) -> (O(x) ∨ P(x))) expresses that everything in set S has property O or P (i.e., 'Everything in that store is either overpriced or poorly made').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the truth table for the conditional to see that ∀x (A -> B) asserts there is no x with A true and B false. This pattern occurs often and should be recognized when translating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity of English quantifier words
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like 'anyone' or 'someone' can mean different quantifiers depending on context (e.g., 'anyone' may mean 'someone' or 'everyone'); careful paraphrasing is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in one sentence 'anyone' meant 'everyone' while in another it meant 'someone'. Determine intended meaning before translating; rephrase into explicit existential/universal structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-theoretic statements via quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Set relations can be written with quantifiers: A ⊆ B as ∀x (x ∈ A -> x ∈ B); disjointness as ¬∃x (x ∈ A ∧ x ∈ (C \ B)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct complex set statements by combining quantifiers and predicate membership; expand definitions (intersection, difference) when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of logical equivalences (De Morgan, distributive, double negation) to transform formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply standard equivalences (double negation, DeMorgan's laws, distributive law, conditional ↔ disjunction/negation equivalences) to show equivalence between different formulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: derive P -> Q ≡ ¬P ∨ Q, show (R -> C) ∧ (S -> C) ≡ (R ∨ S) -> C by using conditional and distributive laws; use such derivations to check equivalence of English formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking truth/falsity of quantified statements: try examples / counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a quantified statement is true or false by testing values or finding counterexamples, working quantifier-by-quantifier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples supplied: evaluate ∀x ∃y (x + y = 5) by exhibiting y for each x; show ∃y ∀x (x + y = 5) false by noting no single y works for all x. For universals, search for a counterexample; for existentials, provide a witness.
